Final-year project · CPU scheduling + reinforcement learning

A scheduler that learns
which scheduler to run,
guided by a real trained LSTM.

Eight classical CPU-scheduling algorithms, a from-scratch NumPy LSTM that predicts burst time from features an OS can actually observe, and a contextual bandit that learns — from a scalar reward, no hand-coded rules — when to trust it. Everything below runs the actual trained weights, not a mock-up.

01 · System overview

Why a meta-scheduler at all

No single classical policy wins on every workload. Shortest-Job-First minimises wait but needs burst time in advance — an oracle privilege no kernel has. This project replaces that oracle with a learned predictor, then learns when to trust it.

01 Workload
Synthetic cpu_bound / interactive / mixed process arrivals, or a real trace CSV.
02 LSTM
32-hidden-unit NumPy LSTM predicts burst time from 4 observable features.
03 Bandit
Contextual bandit reads a 5-feature workload state and picks one scheduler for the episode.
04 Scheduler
FCFS · SJF_Predicted · Round Robin · Priority — whichever the bandit chose — runs to completion.
05 Feedback
Reward = −avg_wait. True bursts retrain the LSTM online. The loop closes.

The honest part

The 4 raw features barely correlate with true burst time (ρ ≈ 0.03). The real signal is process type (ρ ≈ 0.91). So SJF_Predicted is a two-tier estimate — 70% type-based prior, 30% LSTM refinement — not a naive "LSTM predicts burst time" claim.

The result that matters

The bandit was never told SJF-style scheduling is a good idea for heterogeneous workloads. Across 30 independent trials it converges on choosing SJF_Predicted in –% of the states it visits — discovered, not programmed.

04 · Statistical rigor

Is it actually significant?

RL_Adaptive vs. every realistic baseline, both Welch's t-test (parametric) and Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric) — reported as-is, including the cases where they disagree.

Six clean wins

FCFS, RoundRobin, Priority, MLFQ and Lottery are all beaten with both tests agreeing at p < 0.001 and Cohen's d from 1.18 to 2.08 — large to very large effects.

Two honest "mixed" results

Against SJF_Predicted and EDF, the Wilcoxon test is significant but the parametric t-test isn't, with small-to-negligible effect sizes. Reported as mixed, not rounded up to a win.

05 · Beyond average wait

Fairness, tail latency, context-switch cost

Optimising average wait alone can hide starvation or a fragile ranking once preemption isn't free. Both are checked directly.

06 · Stated up front

Limitations, not buried in an appendix

LSTM accuracy is modest

– ticks MAE on a 1–40 tick burst range. Real, but far from oracle-grade — exactly why SJF_Predicted leans on the type prior.

Doesn't beat SJF_Predicted

It matches it. The result is automatic discovery of a known-good policy, not a policy that exceeds a well-tuned heuristic.

EDF comparison is genuinely mixed

Significant under Wilcoxon, not under the t-test, small effect size. Reported as mixed rather than rounded into a win.

Workloads are synthetic

A real-trace loader exists (Google/Alibaba/custom CSV) but no result here is computed from real trace data yet.
